title: At the pharmacy: my head hurts, not me
goal: Explain how you feel to a pharmacist or doctor — using another turned-around pattern: in Russian it isn't you who hurts, it's your body part that hurts you.
bekal: use the pattern У меня болит …
ask for medicine at the pharmacy
use нужно and надо to say you need to

dialogs.title: Диалог — A headache at the pharmacy
dialogs.intro: Ani walks into a pharmacy with a pounding head. Notice that in every complaint, the body part is the subject of the sentence.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Two days. And my throat hurts too.
lines.literal: two — days. and — throat — also — hurts.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.literal: in-the-morning — was — thirty — seven — and — five.

lines.speaker: Аптекарь:
lines.id: That's not high. Have you been in Russia long?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Six months. This is my first winter.

lines.speaker: Аптекарь:
lines.id: I see. You need to rest more and drink hot drinks.
lines.literal: to-you — needed — more — rest — and — drink — hot.

lines.speaker: Аптекарь:
lines.id: This is for your head, and this is for your throat. Three times a day.
lines.literal: here — this — from — head, and — this — from — throat. three — times — in — day.

lines.speaker: Аптекарь:
lines.id: Yes. And if you're not better in three days, go to a doctor.
lines.literal: yes. and — if — through — three — days — not — better — go — to — doctor.

notes: **У меня болит голова literally means "at me hurts head."** ⚠️ The **head** is the subject of the sentence, and the verb болит agrees with the head, not with me. Good news: this is close to English "my head hurts." If more than one thing hurts, the verb goes plural: *У меня болЯТ ноги* (my legs hurt). Learners often try *Я болю*, which doesn't exist in Russian at all.

**Я болею means something different from У меня болит.** *Я болею* = I'm sick (in general, with an illness). *У меня болит голова* = my head hurts (one specific complaint). To say you're calling in sick, use the first: *Я болею* or *Я заболел / заболела* (I've gotten sick).

**От + genitive means "medicine against."** *Таблетки **от** голов**ы*** (headache pills), *лекарство **от** кашл**я*** (cough medicine). Literally "from the head" — the medicine keeps the illness away. ⚠️ Don't use для (for); *лекарство для головы* sounds like something to make your head healthier, not a cure.

**Russians measure body temperature in the armpit, in Celsius.** Normal is 36.6 (about 98 °F). A mild fever starts at 37.0. A truly high one is 38.5 and up. ⚠️ The number 36.6 has a special place in Russian culture — it's a byword for "perfectly healthy," much like 98.6 °F is in the US.

**К + dative means "to (a person)."** *Идите к врачу* (go to the doctor), *Я иду к другу* (I'm going to my friend's). This is the same dative case as in Unit 15, now for going to a person rather than a place.

**Нужно / надо both mean "need to, have to," and are almost interchangeable.** *Вам нужно отдыхать* / *Вам надо отдыхать*. Надо is a bit more casual. Both take the dative for the person: мне надо, тебе нужно, ему надо.

**Через + time means "in (so much time)."** *через три дня* (in three days), *через час* (in an hour), *через неделю* (in a week). Different from **после**, which means "after a specific event": *после еды* (after meals).

grammars.title: У меня болит — the complaint pattern
body: The verb form follows the body part that hurts, not the person.
after: ⚠️ The past form agrees with the gender of the body part, not the person: *болел живот* (masc), *болела голова* (fem), *болело горло* (neut), *болели ноги* (pl). A direct application of the rule from Unit 14.

grammars.title: Parts of the body
body: Dictionary forms in the left column; that's also the form you use in a complaint sentence.
after: ⚠️ Some body parts have irregular plurals: глаз → **глаза**, ухо → **уши**, зуб → **зубы**, нога → **ноги**, рука → **руки**. Worth memorizing, since body parts so often come in pairs.
**Рука** covers both hand and arm; **нога** covers both foot and leg. ⚠️ Russian doesn't split them the way English does (*hand*/*arm*, *foot*/*leg*) — context tells you which one is meant.

blocks.title: A Russian pharmacy works differently
items: **A Russian аптека can give medical advice.** Russian pharmacists are trained and used to recommending medicine for minor complaints without a prescription. Describing your symptoms at the pharmacy is a normal, expected conversation — that's why this unit practices it.
**Скорая (помощь)** is the ambulance, and its number is **103** from a cell phone. The general emergency number **112** works too. ⚠️ Memorize these two numbers before you travel.
**Полис** is a health insurance card. International students must have one; without it, medical care must be paid in full.
**Pharmacy hours:** in big cities many are open 24 hours, marked **круглосуточно** (*kroog-la-SOO-tach-na*) — open around the clock. A long word, but very useful to look for on signs.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the dative form: мне, вам, ему, ей, нам.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: болит — болят — болит — болят — болит — болят
У меня болит голова. — Температура есть? — Три раза в день. — Идите к врачу. — Мне плохо.
У меня болит голова. — Горло тоже болит. — У меня температура. — У меня болят ноги. — Вам нужно отдыхать. — Вызовите скорую!
